How NoteDown's clients talk to the sync server, byte for byte where both
sides have to agree. It implements `docs/sync-and-sharing.md`:
**milestone 1**, sync between the user's own devices (identity, recovery
key, device list, linking and removing devices, the private file), and
**milestone 2**, contacts and shared files, which extends the API of
milestone 1 (decided 2026-10-14). The server is `server/` (`PROJECT.md` →
"Server").

## Encodings

- **Binary values** (keys, signatures, ciphertext) travel as base64url
  without padding (`b64u`).
- **IDs** are `b64u` of 16 bytes (22 characters):
  - identity ID = first 16 bytes of SHA-256 of the identity's public
    signing key (derived, so a restoring device finds its identity from
    the recovery key alone);
  - device ID = the same over the device's public signing key;
  - file ID = 16 random bytes, chosen by the client.
- **Canonical JSON** is what gets signed: object keys sorted by code
  point, no whitespace, UTF-8, only strings, integers and objects
  (Python: `json.dumps(v, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"),
  ensure_ascii=False)`).
- Times in responses are ISO 8601 UTC.

## Keys

| Key | Algorithm | Derived from |
|---|---|---|
| Recovery key | 16 random bytes, shown as 26 characters of RFC 4648 base32 (A–Z, 2–7, no padding) in groups of 4 with a last group of 2 (`XXXX-…-XX`); typed input is case-insensitive and reads 0, 1, 8 as O, I, B | — |
| Identity signing key | Ed25519 | HKDF-SHA256(recovery key, salt `NoteDown`, info `identity-sign`) → 32-byte seed |
| Recovery device keys | Ed25519 + X25519 | same, info `recovery-sign` / `recovery-enc` |
| Device keys | Ed25519 + X25519 | generated on the device, never leave it |
| File key | AES-256-GCM | random per file; renewed when a device is removed, the previous one chained to it ("Version history") |

A 32-byte seed imports into WebCrypto as PKCS#8 (fixed 16-byte prefix
plus the seed); exporting the key as JWK yields the public key.

**Wrapped file key** (opaque to the server, at most 512 characters, as
in HPKE, RFC 9180): `b64u(ephemeral X25519 public key ‖ nonce ‖
AES-GCM(wrap key, file key))`, where the wrap key is HKDF-SHA256 over
the X25519 shared secret with an empty salt and info `notedown-wrap` ‖
ephemeral public key ‖ recipient public key, and the nonce has 12 bytes. **File ciphertext**: 12-byte nonce ‖ AES-GCM of
the padded, compressed Markdown file, a fresh nonce per upload.
Compressed: one `0x01` byte, then the raw DEFLATE stream (RFC 1951, no
zlib header) of the UTF-8 text (`CompressionStream("deflate-raw")` in
the browser); Markdown shrinks to about a third,
which saves storage and quota. Padding (ISO/IEC 7816-4 style, so the
server sees sizes only in 4 KiB steps): one `0x80` byte, then `0x00`
bytes up to the next multiple of 4096 bytes (a plaintext that already is
a multiple gets a full extra block); decrypting strips trailing `0x00`s
and then one `0x80`. Older files are read as they are: a plaintext that
doesn't start with `0x01` is uncompressed UTF-8 (Markdown never starts
with that byte), one without the `0x80` marker is unpadded. App versions
from before compression can't read compressed files, so every device has
to run a current version.

## Device list

An identity's devices are an append-only chain of signed entries:

```json
{"identity": "<id>", "seq": 0, "prev": "", "op": "add",
 "device": {"id": "<device id>", "kind": "device", "sign": "<b64u>", "enc": "<b64u>"},
 "signer": "identity", "sig": "<b64u>"}
```

- `seq` counts from 0; `prev` is `b64u(SHA-256(canonical JSON of the
  previous entry including its sig))`, empty for `seq` 0.
- `op` is `add` (with the full `device`) or `remove` (only
  `{"id": ...}`); `kind` is `device` or `recovery`.
- `signer` is `identity` (the identity key, i.e. whoever holds the
  recovery key) or the ID of a device that is on the list at that point.
  `sig` is the Ed25519 signature over the canonical JSON of the entry
  without `sig`.
- The first entries (genesis) add the first device and the recovery
  device, both signed by `identity`. The recovery device can't be
  removed; a device can remove itself.
- The server checks the whole chain on every append, and every client
  checks it before trusting a key from it.

## Contacts and invitations

Two people become contacts through an **invitation**: one shows its code
or sends its link, the other sends a contact request through it, the
first confirms (decided 2026-10-14: showing a code or sending a link
alone doesn't add anyone). Code and link are the same text:

```
https://<web app>/invite/#v=1&id=<identity id>&s=<secret>&name=<name>&srv=<home server>
```

- `id` is the inviter's identity ID, i.e. the fingerprint of its identity
  key: the requester checks that the identity key the server returns
  hashes to it, so the server can't slip in its own. `s` is 16 random
  bytes (`b64u`), the **invitation secret**; `name` the inviter's display
  name (form-encoded, at most 40 characters, may be empty). The fragment
  never reaches a web server. `srv` is the inviter's **home server**, the
  API address the requester talks to (form-encoded; missing = the default
  server, the app's configured API address, as in older links). As a QR
  code ("My code") it is about 200 characters; the in-app scanner reads it, and a phone's own camera
  opens it like the link.
- The **invitation ID** is `b64u` of the first 16 bytes of SHA-256 of
  the secret. The inviting device creates the invitation under that ID
  and signs it: `sig` is its Ed25519 signature over the UTF-8 bytes of
  `notedown-invite-v1:<invitation id>`. The server never sees the secret.
- A **code** invitation is open for 10 minutes, a **link** invitation for
  7 days; at most 20 are open per identity. It takes one request.
- The **contact request** carries the requester's card, sealed for each
  active device (`kind` `device`) of the inviter's verified device list
  like a relay payload, with the HKDF label `notedown-contact`; the
  plaintext is the UTF-8 JSON `{"v": 1, "identity": "<id>", "name":
  "<display name>", "secret": "<s>"}`.
- The inviter's device shows the request only if the invitation's `sig`
  is from a device on its own verified list, the card's `secret` hashes
  to the invitation ID and its `identity` is the one the server reports.
  So the server can't forge a request, and only someone who had the code
  or link can send one.
- **Confirming** records the two identities as contacts on the server
  and deletes the invitation; **declining** deletes it. An open request
  waits for the inviter up to 30 days. The requester sees the inviter as
  a contact once the server lists the pair (`GET /v1/contacts`).
- Contacts on the server are a symmetric pair of identity IDs and only
  decide who may read whose device list and share a file with whom;
  names, colors and the contact list itself live in the user's private
  file (`docs/file-format.md` → "Contacts"). Removing a contact deletes
  the pair.
- **Who may read a device list** (`GET /v1/identities/{id}`, backlog
  #18): the identity itself, its contacts, identities that share a file
  with it, and a requester holding an open invitation of that identity
  (`?invitation=<invitation id>`). Anyone else gets 404, as for an
  unknown identity.

## Authentication

No accounts and no passwords: a device signs a challenge.

1. `GET /v1/auth/challenge` → `{"challenge": "<b64u>"}`, valid 2 minutes
   (stateless: time, random bytes and a server MAC).
2. `POST /v1/auth/token` with `{"identity", "device", "challenge",
   "sig"}`; `sig` is the device's Ed25519 signature over the UTF-8 bytes
   of `notedown-auth-v1:<challenge>`. → `{"token", "expires"}`, valid one
   hour.
3. Every authenticated request sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
   The server also checks on each request that the device is still on
   the list, so a removed device is locked out at once.

### Blocked and deleted identities

Backlog #34: the admin can block an identity, with or without an end,
and delete it ("Admin"); the user deletes their own identity with the
recovery key (below).

- **Blocked:** the token endpoint and every authenticated request of the
  identity's devices answer **423 `{"detail": "identity is blocked",
  "until": "<iso>" | null}`** (`null`: no end) until the block is lifted
  or its end has passed. Nothing is deleted, and the other identities go
  on syncing the files they share with it.
- **Deleted:** its files that no other remaining identity is a member of
  (with their stored states), its devices' wrapped keys, its device list,
  contacts and invitations are deleted. Files it shares with others stay
  for them with the same members, so their notes and circles don't
  change. Only a row with its ID and identity key stays, marked deleted:
  it keeps those member sets intact, and the token endpoint and every
  request of its devices answer **410 `{"detail": "identity deleted"}`**,
  so its other devices learn what happened. A member reading its device
  list (`GET /v1/identities/{id}`) gets `{"identity_key", "entries": [],
  "deleted": true}`: no devices to wrap keys for. A deleted member counts
  against no limit. The ID can't be registered again.
- **Deleting it yourself:** `POST /v1/identities/{id}/delete` with
  `{"challenge", "sig"}`, where `challenge` comes from `GET
  /v1/auth/challenge` and `sig` is the **identity key's** Ed25519
  signature over the UTF-8 bytes of `notedown-delete-v1:<challenge>`.
  So only whoever holds the recovery key can delete, also without a
  device and while blocked. → 204 (also when already deleted); 403 for a
  signature that doesn't match the identity key (a device key is not
  enough); 404 for an unknown identity; 400 for an invalid or expired
  challenge.

## Endpoints

| Method and path | Auth | Request → response |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | — | → `{"ok": true}` when the database answers |
| `GET /health/live` | — | → `{"ok": true}` without touching the database (the uptime check, so Neon can sleep) |
| `POST /v1/identities` | — | `{"identity_key", "entries": [genesis…]}` → 201 `{"id"}`; 409 if it exists |
| `GET /v1/identities/{id}` | yes | `?invitation=<invitation id>` optional → `{"identity_key", "entries"}`, for a deleted identity also `"deleted": true` with no entries; 404 unless the caller may read it ("Contacts and invitations") |
| `POST /v1/identities/{id}/delete` | identity key | `{"challenge", "sig"}` → 204: deletes the identity ("Blocked and deleted identities") |
| `POST /v1/identities/{id}/entries` | device of `{id}` | `{"entry"}` → 201 `{"seq"}`; 409 `{"detail", "seq"}` when `seq`/`prev` is not the current end |
| `GET /v1/files` | yes | → `{"files": [{"id", "version", "updated", "size", "members", "history"}], "quota", "max_members", "epoch", "news", "deleted"}`: every file the identity is a member of, in code point order of the ID; `size` is the decoded ciphertext in bytes, `members` the sorted identity IDs, `history` whether the file keeps older states ("Version history"), `quota` the caller's storage limit (so the app can show the usage; "Limits"), `epoch` the restore epoch or `null` until the first restore ("Admin"), `news` the news version or `null` until the first change ("Admin" → "News"), `deleted` the sorted IDs of the deleted identities among the members of these files ("Blocked and deleted identities"), `max_members` the most members a file the caller creates may have ("Limits") |
| `GET /v1/news` | yes | → `{"version", "news": [{"id", "created", "modified", "body"}]}`: the owner's published posts, unencrypted and the same for everybody ("Admin" → "News"); any identity may read it |
| `GET /v1/files/{fid}` | yes | → `{"id", "version", "ciphertext", "key"}`, `key` wrapped for the calling device (or `null`) |
| `PUT /v1/files/{fid}` | yes | `{"base_version", "ciphertext", "keys"?, "members"?, "previous_key"?, "restore"?}` → `{"version"}`; 409 `{"detail", "version"}` if `base_version` is not the server's version, 409 `{"detail": "file exists", "id", "version"}` if a new file's member set already has a file |
| `GET /v1/files/{fid}/versions` | yes | → `{"key_gen", "versions": [{"version", "updated", "replaced", "size", "key_gen", "pinned", "saved"}], "chain": [{"gen", "sealed"}]}`: the stored older states, newest first, and the key chain ("Version history"); 404 unless the caller is a member |
| `POST /v1/files/{fid}/versions` | yes | → `{"version", "saved"}`: "Back up now", stores the current state as a state of the history ("Version history"); `saved` false when it is stored already; 404 unless the caller is a member, 409 `{"detail": "no version history"}` when the file keeps none |
| `GET /v1/files/{fid}/versions/{v}` | yes | → `{"id", "version", "ciphertext", "key_gen"}`; 404 for a state that isn't stored (the current version included) or a non-member |
| `POST /v1/files/{fid}/keys` | yes | `{"keys": {device id: wrapped key}}` → 204; adds or replaces keys without a new version (linking a device) |
| `POST /v1/invitations` | yes | `{"id", "kind", "sig"}` (`kind` `code` or `link`) → 201 `{"expires"}`; 400 for an invalid ID, kind or a `sig` that isn't the calling device's signature, 409 if the ID exists, 413 with 20 open |
| `GET /v1/invitations` | yes | → `{"invitations": [{"id", "kind", "device", "sig", "expires", "request"}]}` of the identity; `device` is the signing device, `request` `null` or `{"identity", "card"}` with the card sealed for the calling device (`null` if none is) |
| `DELETE /v1/invitations/{iid}` | yes | → 204: the inviter withdraws it or declines its request (also when it is gone; nothing happens for anyone else) |
| `POST /v1/invitations/{iid}/request` | yes | `{"cards": {device id: sealed card}}` → 204; 404 unknown or expired, 409 already requested, 403 own invitation, 400 for no card, a card over 512 characters or not `b64u`, or a device that isn't an active device of the inviter |
| `GET /v1/contacts` | yes | → `{"contacts": [identity id]}` |
| `POST /v1/contacts` | yes | `{"invitation"}` → 201 `{"identity"}`: confirms the request on one's own invitation; 404 without one |
| `DELETE /v1/contacts/{id}` | yes | → 204 (also when they were no contact) |
| `POST /v1/relay` | — | → 201 `{"slot", "expires"}`, a 10-minute mailbox |
| `PUT /v1/relay/{slot}` | yes | `{"payload"}` → 204, once (409 after that) |
| `GET /v1/relay/{slot}` | — | → 200 `{"payload"}` (and the slot is gone), 204 while empty, 404 when gone or expired |

- **Members:** every identity of a file's `members` may read and upload
  it and add keys; to anyone else it is unknown (404). The set is fixed
  when the file is created and never changes (`docs/sync-and-sharing.md`
  → "Files"); the private file is the file of the set of one.
- **Upload** (`PUT /v1/files/{fid}`): `base_version` 0 creates the file
  and needs `keys`, and may name `members` (the caller plus contacts of
  the caller, at most the caller's member limit ("Limits"), no
  duplicates; default: the caller alone; 400 if malformed, without the
  caller or too many, 403 if one is no contact of the caller). On later uploads `members` may be left out or must be the
  file's set (400 otherwise). Each member set has at most one
  file: creating a second answers 409 with the existing file's `id` and
  `version`, so two devices sharing at the same time don't split it.
  With `keys` the whole set of wrapped keys is replaced (renewing the
  file key after a device was removed); without, the keys stay. Every key
  must belong to an active device of a member. Renewing an existing file
  needs `previous_key`, the replaced key sealed with the new one (400
  without; at most 512 characters, `b64u`), which the server adds to the
  key chain. `"restore": true` marks an upload that brings back an older
  state: the state it replaces is pinned ("Version history").
- Removing a device also deletes its wrapped keys in every file.
- **Linking a device:** the new device creates a relay slot and shows a
  QR code with its device keys and the slot. The linked device appends
  the new device to the list, adds its wrapped file keys and puts the
  identity ID and the display name, encrypted for the new device's
  `enc` key, into the slot. The new device polls the slot (every 2 s),
  then authenticates normally. Formats (client side,
  `app/js/core/linking.js`):
  - **QR code text:** `notedown:link?v=1&slot=<slot>&sign=<b64u>&enc=<b64u>&name=<name>&srv=<server>`
    — a URL query (form-encoded), the device's public Ed25519 and X25519
    keys, its suggested name (at most 40 characters, may be empty) and
    `srv`, the server the slot is on (missing = the default server).
    About 210 characters: QR version 10 at error correction M.
  - **Relay payload:** b64u of ephemeral X25519 public key ‖ nonce ‖
    AES-256-GCM ciphertext, built like a wrapped file key but with the
    HKDF label `notedown-relay` instead of `notedown-wrap`; the plaintext
    is the UTF-8 JSON `{"v": 1, "identity": "<id>", "name": "<display name>", "server": "<home server>"}`;
    `server` is where the identity lives, where the new device signs in
    (missing = the default server).
  - The linked device first reads the slot (204 = still open) so an
    expired code fails before the device list changes. The new device
    joins only if its own device is active on the verified list of
    that identity.
- **Restoring with the recovery key:** derive the identity and recovery
  device keys, authenticate as the recovery device, append the new
  device, wrap the file keys for it.
- Errors are `{"detail": "<message>"}` with 400 (malformed), 401 (no or
  invalid token), 403 (not allowed), 404, 409 (conflict), 413 (too
  large, or the storage quota is used up), 429 (rate limit; the
  `Retry-After` header gives the seconds until the window ends).

## Version history

Backlog #7. A file keeps its older states while **one of its members**
has version history switched on; the admin switches it per identity
("Admin"), the basis of a paid option later (backlog #33). Every member
of such a file may list and read its states, also one without the
switch. The server only stores and thins the encrypted states; reading,
comparing and restoring happen on the device.

- **Stored:** each upload of an existing file stores the state it
  replaces (table `file_versions`: `version`, `ciphertext`, `updated` =
  when that state was uploaded, `replaced` = now, `key_gen`, `pinned`,
  `saved`).
  Not counted against the storage quota; the admin page shows its size.
- **Thinning** on every such upload: for states replaced in the last
  24 hours one per hour, before that one per UTC day — in each hour or
  day the first state replaced in it, i.e. the one from before that
  hour's or day's changes. Pinned states stay; states saved by hand
  don't count as the first of their hour or day. Nothing stays longer than
  30 days after it was replaced (listing and reading leave out what is
  older even before the next upload deletes it).
- **Key chain:** a file's key has a generation, `key_gen`, 1 at creation
  and + 1 with every renewal. Renewing stores the previous key sealed
  with the new one (`previous_key`, table `file_key_chain`: `gen` = the
  generation of the sealed key), so a device that has the current key
  opens the key of any older state: b64u of 12-byte nonce ‖ AES-GCM(new
  file key, previous file key) with the associated data
  `notedown-previous-key` (`sealPreviousKey` in `app/js/core/crypto.js`).
  A removed device gets no newer key and so nothing new either.
- **Restoring** is an ordinary upload of the older state's notes on top
  of the current version, with `"restore": true`: the server pins the
  state it replaces, so the restore can be undone; the other devices
  merge it as any change (`docs/sync-and-sharing.md` → "Version
  history").
- **Back up now** (`POST /v1/files/{fid}/versions`) copies the current
  version into the history at once, pinned and `saved`, with
  `replaced` = now (so it is kept 30 days from then); its `version` is
  the file's current one until the next upload, which keeps that copy
  instead of storing the state again. Calling it again without a change
  stores nothing (`"saved": false`). The app calls it for every file
  with a history.
- **Switching it off** for an identity deletes the stored states of the
  files of which no member has it any more; later uploads store none.

## Admin

For the server's owner. Every endpoint below needs the usual bearer token
and answers **404 `{"detail": "not found"}`** unless the caller's identity
ID is listed in the environment variable `ADMIN_IDENTITIES` (IDs separated
by commas or white space; empty or unset: nobody). That holds for a missing
or invalid token and for a request body that doesn't parse as well, so
nobody else learns the endpoints exist. Only exact IDs match; anything
else in the variable (a typo, `*`) is ignored. Every device of an admin
identity is an admin. The admin endpoints record nothing new about
identities or devices: they show what the tables hold (no last-seen times,
no request logs).

| Method and path | Request → response |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/admin/overview` | → `{"identity", "counts": {"identities", "devices", "files", "shared_files", "contacts", "invitations", "news", "blocked"}, "storage": {"files", "history", "database", "database_limit"}, "quota"}`; `storage.history` is the decoded ciphertext of all stored older states; `devices` counts active devices of kind `device` (no recovery devices), `shared_files` the files with more than one member, `contacts` each pair once, `invitations` the open ones, `news` the published (not archived) posts, `blocked` the identities blocked now; `identities` leaves deleted ones out; `storage.files` is the decoded ciphertext of all files in bytes, `database` the database size, `database_limit` the host's size limit in bytes from the server's configuration (`DATABASE_LIMIT_MB`; Postgres can't report it), `null` when that isn't set or isn't a whole number above 0 (the server starts anyway and logs a warning); `quota` the default quota; `max_members` the server-wide member limit, `max_members_override` the stored one or `null` (= the default, 20) |
| `GET /v1/admin/identities` | → `{"identities": [{"id", "created", "devices", "files", "used", "quota", "quota_override", "updated", "contacts", "history", "blocked", "blocked_until", "max_members", "max_members_override"}]}`, newest first, deleted identities left out; `blocked` whether a block holds now, `blocked_until` its end (`null`: none, or not blocked); `history` whether version history is switched on; `used` is what the quota counts (the decoded ciphertext of the files it is a member of), `quota` the effective quota, `quota_override` the stored one or `null`, `updated` the newest `updated` of its files (`null` without files), `max_members` the effective member limit of the files it creates, `max_members_override` its own or `null` (= the server-wide one) |
| `GET /v1/admin/identities/{id}` | → `{"id", "created", "used", "quota", "quota_override", "history", "history_size", "devices": [{"id", "kind", "active"}], "files": [{"id", "version", "updated", "size", "members"}], "contacts": [id], "invitations", "blocked", "blocked_until", "max_members", "max_members_override"}`; devices in the order they were added to the list, files newest first; `history_size` is the decoded ciphertext of the stored states of its files; 404 for an unknown or deleted identity |
| `PUT /v1/admin/identities/{id}/quota` | `{"quota": <bytes> \| null}` → 204; `null` resets to the default; 400 unless `1 <= quota <= 1 GiB`; 404 for an unknown identity |
| `PUT /v1/admin/max-members` | `{"max_members": <2..50> \| null}` → 204: the server-wide member limit ("Limits"); `null` resets to the default 20; 400 otherwise |
| `PUT /v1/admin/identities/{id}/max-members` | `{"max_members": <2..50> \| null}` → 204: the member limit of the files this identity creates; `null` = the server-wide one; 400 otherwise; 404 for an unknown or deleted identity |
| `PUT /v1/admin/identities/{id}/history` | `{"history": true \| false}` → 204: switches version history on or off ("Version history"); 400 for anything but a boolean; 404 for an unknown identity |
| `PUT /v1/admin/identities/{id}/block` | `{"blocked": true \| false, "until"?: "<iso>"}` → 204: blocks the identity, until `until` (a time with zone, ahead) or without an end, or lifts the block ("Blocked and deleted identities"); 400 for a non-boolean `blocked`, a bad or past `until`, or `until` without `blocked`; 404 for an unknown or deleted identity; 409 for an admin identity |
| `DELETE /v1/admin/identities/{id}` | → 204: deletes the identity as described in "Blocked and deleted identities"; 404 for an unknown or already deleted identity; 409 for an admin identity |
| `GET /v1/admin/news` | → `{"news": [{"id", "created", "modified", "body", "archived"}]}`, newest `created` first, archived posts included |
| `POST /v1/admin/news` | `{"body"}` → 201 `{"id", "created", "modified"}`: a new, published post; 400 for a bad body, 409 `{"detail": "too many news"}` ("Limits") |
| `PUT /v1/admin/news/{id}` | `{"body"?, "archived"?}` → 204; `modified` is set to now only when `body` differs from the stored one, `archived` hides a post from the feed or publishes it again; 400 for neither field, a bad body or a non-boolean `archived`; 404 for an unknown ID; 409 `too many news` when publishing it again would exceed 20 published posts |
| `DELETE /v1/admin/news/{id}` | → 204 (also when it is gone) |
| `GET /v1/admin/backup` | → the backup file (below), `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="notedown-backup-<YYYY-MM-DD-HHMM>.json"` (UTC) |
| `POST /v1/admin/restore` | a backup → 200 `{"identities", "files"}` (the numbers restored); 400, 409 (below) |

**Backup format.** One consistent snapshot (a single `REPEATABLE READ`
read-only transaction), a JSON document
`{"format": "notedown-backup", "version": 1, "created": "<iso>", "tables": {…}}`.
`tables` holds an array of row objects per table, with these columns
(binary values `b64u`, times ISO 8601 UTC):

| Table | Columns |
|---|---|
| `identities` | `id`, `identity_key`, `created`, `quota` (override or `null`), `history` (optional: missing = off), `blocked`, `blocked_until`, `deleted` (optional: missing = not blocked, not deleted; a deleted identity has no device list, every other one has one), `max_members` (optional: missing = `null`) |
| `device_entries` | `identity_id`, `seq`, `entry` (the signed entry as in "Device list") |
| `files` | `id`, `owner`, `version`, `ciphertext`, `updated`, `member_key`, `key_gen` (optional: missing = 1) |
| `file_versions` | `file_id`, `version` (below the file's; equal for a `saved` one), `ciphertext`, `updated`, `replaced`, `key_gen` (at most the file's), `pinned`, `saved` (optional: missing = false); optional table |
| `file_key_chain` | `file_id`, `gen` (below the file's `key_gen`), `sealed`; optional table |
| `file_members` | `file_id`, `identity_id` |
| `file_keys` | `file_id`, `device_id`, `wrapped` |
| `contacts` | `a`, `b` (both directions, as stored) |
| `invitations` | `id`, `identity_id`, `kind`, `device_id`, `sig`, `expires`, `requester`, `requested_at`, `cards` |
| `news` | `id`, `body`, `created`, `modified`, `archived`; optional: a backup without it (older ones) restores with no news |

Not in it: `devices` (derived from the device lists), relay slots, rate
limit counters and the server state (the epoch, the news version and
the server-wide member limit, which a restore leaves as it is). The file is as sensitive
as the database: it holds the encrypted files and the public device lists.

**Restore** replaces everything in one transaction, so a failed restore
changes nothing:

- The document is checked first: 400 for a wrong `format` or unsupported
  `version`, a missing table, a row with other columns than listed, a
  malformed or dangling value, or a device list that doesn't verify (every
  identity's list goes through the same check as `POST /v1/identities`; a
  file's `member_key` must match its members).
- 409 `{"detail": "the backup would lock you out"}` when the calling
  identity is not in the backup or the calling device is not active on its
  list there: the admin could not sign in afterwards.
- Then every table (relay slots and rate limit counters too) is emptied,
  the backup's rows are inserted from a fixed list of columns per table
  (never from the JSON keys), `devices` is rebuilt from the verified lists
  a new random **restore epoch** is stored and the news version is renewed. Tokens stay valid for
  devices that are active in the backup.
- Devices linked after the backup are not on the restored list and have to
  be linked again; so are identities created after it (they are gone).
- The request body is at most 32 MB (Cloud Run's limit), which is the
  largest backup that can be restored; the code doesn't enforce it.

**Restore epoch.** `GET /v1/files` returns the epoch (16 random bytes,
`b64u`; `null` until the first restore). A client remembers it per server.
When the server's epoch differs from the remembered one, or the server
lists a file at a lower version than the client has seen (a restore
without an epoch, such as the database host's own point-in-time
recovery), the client treats the server as restored: all its file records
for that server start over (`version` 0, empty base) so everything it
holds is merged with the server's. No note on a device is lost; notes
deleted since the backup may come back, and a note edited on both sides
becomes a conflict copy. A file the restored server no longer has is
created again. The client's side is `app/js/sync/files.js`.

**News.** The owner publishes posts (changelog, announcements, a call to
take part in a poll) to everybody using the server, from the admin page.
They are plain Markdown, **not encrypted** (official communication, the
same for every identity) and live in the table `news` (`id` as other IDs,
`body`, `created`, `modified`, `archived`). The **news version** is an
opaque string (16 random bytes, `b64u`) in the server state, renewed with
every change that is made (a post created, its body changed, archived,
published again, deleted, and a restore; not by a request that changes
nothing) and `null` until the first one. `GET /v1/files` carries it, so a
client fetches `GET /v1/news` only when it differs from the one it
remembers. The feed lists the posts that are not archived, newest
`created` first, times ISO 8601 UTC. `modified` changes only with the
body (not on archive or publish again), so a client can compare it for
equality to see an edit. An archived or deleted post is gone from the
feed for everyone.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Storage per identity (decoded ciphertext of all files it is a member of, shared ones in full) | 2 MB, or the admin's override per identity (1 byte to 1 GiB) |
| Files per identity (it is a member of) | 50 |
| Open invitations per identity | 20 |
| Members per file | 20, or what the admin sets for the server or the creating identity (2 to 50) |
| Sealed card | 512 characters each |
| Devices on a list (active) | 20 |
| Relay payload | 8 KB |
| News post body | 1 byte to 16 KiB (UTF-8), not only white space |
| Published (not archived) news posts | 20 |
| News posts in total (archived ones included) | 200 |
| `POST /v1/identities` | 10 per day per IP address |
| `POST /v1/relay` | 30 per hour per IP address |

Storage quota and file count are checked on `PUT /v1/files/{id}` for
**every member** of the file, since a shared file counts in full for each
of them (backlog #27; so the usage the app shows is the one enforced).
The replaced file's old size doesn't count. Over a limit the upload
answers 413 `{"detail": "storage quota exceeded" | "too many files",
"members": [<identity IDs over the limit>]}`, so the app can say whose
storage is full. The default quota is one constant; the admin can set a
different quota per identity ("Admin"), the basis for a paid option later.
Each member is checked against its own quota, and `GET /v1/files` returns
the caller's.

The member limit is checked only when a file is created, against the
creating identity's limit: its own override, else the server-wide one
(`server_state` key `max_members`), else 20; over it the upload answers
400 `{"detail": "too many members"}`. A file's members never change, so
a lower limit later leaves existing files as they are. `GET /v1/files`
returns the caller's limit, which the app's share dialog applies.

A news post over its size or an empty one is a 400; publishing one that
would make 21 published or 201 in total (`POST`, or `PUT` with
`"archived": false`) answers 409 `{"detail": "too many news"}`.

The rate limits count per client IP in fixed windows (counters in
Postgres, shared by all server instances); IPv6 addresses count per /64
prefix. The client IP is the last entry of `X-Forwarded-For`, which
Cloud Run's front end appends (earlier entries come from the client and
can be forged), or the socket peer without that header. Authenticated
calls and reads are not limited. The environment variable
`RATE_LIMITS=off` disables the limits (tests, the local end-to-end run).
